summary:
Latvia has no dedicated statute on legal gender recognition. The law does not define "sex change"; on the available account an identity-document change has been granted on presentation of a medical certificate. In 2008 the Supreme Court held that authorities should have granted recognition to a transgender person refused one in 2004 after a partial sex change. A 2009 Saeima proposal that would have required sterilisation as a condition of changing legal gender was rejected. Nonbinary identity is not recognised. In June 2025 coalition members of the Saeima said trans rights "have not emerged as a major issue yet."

Same-sex conduct is not criminalised: male homosexuality was decriminalised in 1992, female homosexuality was never criminalised, and the age of consent was equalised at 16 in 1999.

One trans immigrant told LSM that acquiring legal recognition of his gender would invalidate both his marriage and his residency status, tying document change to immigration exposure.

Registered partnerships, codified in November 2023 and in force since 1 July 2024, carry rights similar to marriage except for adoption and inheritance. A 2006 constitutional amendment defines marriage as a union between a man and a woman. In April 2023 the Saeima amended the Law on the Protection of the Children's Rights to bar adoption of Latvian children by foreign same-sex couples, a provision that reaches a trans visitor whose relationship is read as same-sex under local law.

Enforcement of hate-motivated offences is the main documented protection gap. In Hanovs v. Latvia the European Court of Human Rights found unanimously on 18 July 2024 that Articles 3, 8 and 14 had been violated after a 2020 homophobic attack in Riga: no criminal charges were brought although the aggressor admitted anti-gay slurs, and the case was downgraded to a minor public-order matter with a lenient fine. The Prosecutor General reopened the criminal proceedings after the ruling.

In a separate case, two people were attacked in Daugavpils; police closed the investigation and the Prosecutor General ordered it reopened. Homophobic posts by former MEP Mamikins were investigated; he left for Russia.

Anti-discrimination protection documented for Latvia covers sexual orientation in employment; no provision addressing gender identity is documented.
tangentialFactors:
ILGA-Europe ranked Latvia 24th of 27 European Union member states for LGBT rights protection in 2023.

The European Court of Human Rights judgment restates states' positive obligations to investigate and punish hate crimes thoroughly; the Strasbourg Observers analysis reads it as a clarification of those duties.

An administrative court overturned the denial of asylum to a Ghanaian LGBTI seeker.

A small gay scene exists in Riga; outside the capital the sparse population supports none, and the bars, clubs, shops and libraries established since the restoration of independence are concentrated there.
localsOnly:
The Ombudsman's 2018 call for a partnership law cited that about half of Latvian children are born outside marriage and should have legal protections.

Any person over 25 may adopt, but two people not married to each other may not adopt the same child, so in an unmarried couple only one partner can adopt.

Lesbian couples can access IVF and assisted insemination treatment.

A 2020 court ruling on parental leave for same-sex couples led to a Justice Ministry draft civil union law in 2022.

In September 2006 the Saeima passed Labour Code amendments prohibiting workplace discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation; President Vaira Vīķe-Freiberga refused to sign the bill until that protection was added.
outOfScopeNotes:
Enforcement after the reopened proceedings in the Hanovs and Daugavpils cases is unresolved; no outcome is recorded in the available sources.

No education-specific findings appear in the available sources.

No sourced material addresses police treatment of transgender people specifically, bathroom or facilities access rules, or border screening practices.
